Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health

Dear Administrator Dr. Oz, 
As the longtime national, nonpartisan health care consumer advocacy organization, Families 
USA appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 2026 Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization proposed rule. For 45 years, Families USA has worked toward our vision of a 
health care system in which everyone in America has access to high-quality, affordable coverage 
and care that protects their health and financial security. If finalized, this rule will take essential 
steps toward that goal by providing standards and transparency around prior authorization the 
over 142 million people who rely on Medicaid, Medicare, and marketplace coverage for their 
health coverage.1 Families USA generally supports the proposed rule and offers constructive 
feedback to assist the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) in strengthening some 
of the provisions finalizing the regulation.  
National data-sharing and interoperability standards are critical to reducing waste, enabling 
real-time coordination of services across health sectors, and driving meaningful improvements 
in health care quality and outcomes for our nationâ€™s families. By allowing health and health care 
data to flow more smoothly within and across the health care system, providers can better 
identify and bridge potential gaps in care and drive needed improvements in the quality and 
value of health care services. Moreover, achieving seamless data sharing across the health care 
system can be vital to helping providers and payers effectively use utilization management tools 
like prior authorization, which, if implemented carefully, can both protect patients from 
unnecessary, costly, and low-value care and avoid delaying or denying medically necessary care 
that patients truly need.  
The proposed rule makes important, albeit incremental, steps to improve data flow within the 
current system. Ultimately, CMS, in collaboration with Congress, should establish a national 
digital heath record that guarantees every patient has access to comprehensive, up-to-date 
2 
 
information on their health and health care â€“ which readily follows the patient across the health 
care system regardless of their insurer and provider. Moreover, health insurers should be held 
accountable to a standardized timely process for administering and approving coverage 
decisions, including prior authorization requests. Ultimately, health insurersâ€™ use of prior 
authorization and other utilization management tools should never result in health care 
consumers being denied medically necessary care and coverage.  
Families USA offers specific comments on five sections of the proposed rule. If finalized, these 
proposals would both expand existing national data-sharing and interoperability standards 
related to the use of prior authorizations for prescription and physician administered drugs as 
well as strengthen prior authorization related safeguards that help ensure consumersâ€™ timely 
access to medically necessary care.

II. B. Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Families USA supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require all impacted payers2 to adopt expanded Prior 
Authorization Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) that require additional technology-
related standards to facilitate electronic prior authorization for physician administered drugs 
covered under a medical benefit3 and prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit.4 
Specifically, these proposals would require payers to adopt technology standards that allow 
payers and providers to electronically share prior authorization coverage and documentation 
requirements for drugs, beginning on October 1, 2027, facilitating quicker appeals or alternate 
treatment plans for patients.  
Prior authorization is a process by which a payer requires approval for a certain service or 
medication before the plan will cover it.5 When used appropriately and effectively, this tool can 
reduce patient exposure to unnecessary, low-quality, or high-cost care. 6 However, insurersâ€™ 
misuse and overuse of prior authorization often interferes with consumersâ€™ ability to access the 
care they need in a timely, efficient manner. About 1 in 6 insured patients across insurer types 
3 
 
report a variety of problems stemming from their insurerâ€™s use of prior authorization.7 For 
example, 37 percent of these patients reported paying more than they expected for their care, 
26 percent reported a decline in health, 32 percent reported significant delays in receiving the 
care they need, and 34 percent reported not being able to receive the care their provider 
recommended at all.8 Among privately insured patients, 21 percent of adults report that they or 
a family member have been denied care their doctor recommended in the past year, and 41 
percent who experienced a denial said it led to a delay in care.9  
Importantly, beneficiaries covered by many of the payers that would be impacted by this rule 
were more likely to report challenges with their insurerâ€™s prior authorization processes than the 
national average: 17 percent of marketplace enrollees, and more than one in five (22 percent) 
of Medicaid beneficiaries.10 Similarly, patients taking prescription drugs were more than twice 
as likely to report prior authorization problems than those not taking any.11 
Health care providers similarly report issues with prior authorization. In a 2024 survey of 
physicians, nearly 60 percent reported that prior authorization â€œalwaysâ€ (15 percent) or â€œoftenâ€ 
(42 percent) led to delays in care, and roughly one in five physicians reported that prior 
authorization always or often resulted in patients abandoning their recommended care.12 
If finalized, CMSâ€™ proposal would put in place standard data protocols and related data sharing 
requirements that would allow application developers to create new and refined health 
applications that empower patients, providers, and other payers with electronic access to 
additional health care data and processes, including prior authorization related processes. 
Importantly, by requiring payers to adopt certain standards that allow prior authorization 
processes to occur electronically, CMS can significantly improve the speed and efficiency that 
payers process prior authorization requests for drugs. Adopting electronic prior authorization 
for other types of services has been shown to reduce the median time between a provider 
request for prior authorization and the insurer decision from 18.7 hours to 5.7 hours.13 These 
requirements will be particularly important for patients with time sensitive conditions, ensuring 
they can access their coverage for drug related treatments and therapies as soon as possible 
with minimal care delays.14 
As such, Families USA supports CMSâ€™ proposal to expand the existing electronic prior 
authorization requirements to prescription drugs for impacted payers. Electronic prior 
authorization helps patients more quickly access the prescription drugs they need and saves 
time and money currently spent on administrative costs. 
II. C. Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
2. Proposed Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial in Response to Prior 
Authorization Request for All Drugs.  
Families USA supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to provide a specific reason to 
providers for why a prior authorization request was denied and what actions must be taken to 
resubmit or appeal the decision, for prior authorization requests covering prescription drugs.15 
However, CMS does not set specific guidelines for what those reasons must be in order to 
4 
 
achieve compliance with this proposed reporting requirement â€“ we encourage CMS to provide 
additional detail to strengthen this proposal.  
Health insurer denials of care due to prior authorization are widespread, yet when these denied 
claims are appealed, they are often overturned. For example, in 2024, Medicare Advantage 
plans denied roughly 8 percent of prior authorization requests, yet among those that were 
appealed, over 80 percent were overturned,16 raising serious concerns that insurers are 
instituting overly aggressive prior authorization requests and are denying medically necessary 
care inappropriately.17 A recent survey by the Commonwealth Fund found that 13 percent of 
privately insured patients had care denied via prior authorization, and 30 percent of appeals 
eventually led to approval.18 The same survey found that nearly 80 percent of patients waited 
two weeks or more for a decision on their appeal.19  
This proposed rule extends the requirement for payers to provide a specific reason when 
denying a prior authorization request to prescription drugs, following previous rulemaking 
establishing a similar requirement for all non-drug services. This is a necessary and helpful 
policy change, as many claims denials are not evidence-based and many health care providers 
report a lack of clarity around whether a particular drug requires prior authorization.20 Ensuring 
that patients and providers know why a request for prior authorization was denied will help 
prevent inappropriate denials of prior authorization and ultimately improve patient access to 
needed prescription drugs on a timely basis.  
For non-drug services where this requirement is already in place, payers have discretion in the 
reasons that they state for the prior authorization denial. As this requirement is extended to 
drug services, CMS provides examples of a â€œspecific reasonâ€ such as documentation that 
doesnâ€™t support the medication or the drug being deemed unnecessary.21 But these examples 
are not definitive guidance to establish reasonable criteria, and without that specificity it will be 
difficult to rein in inappropriate denials of care. CMS should establish clear requirements for 
what information must be included when a payer denies a claim, for both drug and non-drug 
services. 
Clear and standardized communication of the reasoning for a care denial is important for both 
the patient and the provider, as it provides them with a path forward to find an alternative 
treatment or understand what information is needed to appeal the denial.22 Families USA 
supports the proposed requirement to extend existing prior authorization decision 
requirements to prescription drugs and encourages CMS to more explicitly outline what type 
of information would constitute a â€œspecific reason.â€ Further, Families USA recommends that 
CMS place an emphasis on requiring clinical criteria to support denials. 
3. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes.  
Families USA also supports the proposal by CMS to require impacted payers to respond to prior 
authorization requests within standard timeframes based on service and payer type. These 
proposed requirements are: 
â€¢ Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchange (FFE) must 
respond to prior authorization requests for non-drug items and services within 7 days, or 
5 
 
72 hours for an expedited request. This is the same requirement for other impacted 
payers related to non-drug items and services.23 
â€¢ QHPs on the FFE must respond to prior authorization requests for prescription drugs 
within 72 hours, or 24 hours for an expedited request.24 
â€¢ Childrenâ€™s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) fee-for-service programs must respond to 
prior authorization requests for prescription drugs within 24 hours, including expedited 
requests. This is the same requirement for Medicaid fee-for-service programs, Medicaid 
managed care organizations, and CHIP managed care entities.25 
Under current regulations, many impacted payers do not have a consistent requirement to 
respond to prior authorization requests in a timely manner. For example, QHP issuers have no 
requirement to respond to prior authorization requests related to prescription drugs or non-
drug items and services, and requirements for CHIP plans vary depending on whether the 
program is fee-for-service or managed care. The proposed rule is a strong step toward ensuring 
every patientâ€™s prior authorization requests, regardless of their insurer, are addressed without 
needless delay.  
Delays in care like those associated with prior authorization have a real impact on patient 
welfare. Nearly one in five physicians reported that prior authorization has led to a life-
threatening event or intervention to maintain patient health.26 Establishing timeframes for 
payers to respond to prior authorization requests will help avoid unnecessary delays, connecting 
patients with the prescription drugs they need or enabling an appeal of a denial more quickly.  
Families USA supports these changes and urges CMS to adopt the proposed timeframes, if not 
make them tighter. Ensuring that patients receive a timely response to their providersâ€™ 
requests for prior authorization removes delays for prescriptions which are approved as 
medically necessary and helps providers more quickly appeal or prescribe alternative 
medications for requests which are denied. As discussed later in this comment, we also urge 
CMS to issue joint rulemaking with the Department of Labor to further standardize prior 
authorization timelines for patients across all payer types. This standardization should 
prioritize the most consumer-friendly timeline from existing standards, such as requiring all 
prescription drug prior authorization determinations to be made within 24 hours. 
5. Proposed Changes to Reporting Deadlines and Reporting Levels for Publicly Reported Prior 
Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and Services for Medicaid Managed Care Plans and 
CHIP Managed Care Entities;  
6. Proposed Changes to Publicly Reported Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and 
Services for Impacted Payers; and  
7. Proposed Requirement to Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics for Drugs and 
Impacted Payers.  
Families USA supports the proposed updates to the metrics related to prior authorization that 
impacted payers must public report. Specifically, CMS proposes multiple updates to the publicly 
reported prior authorization metrics including: 
6 
 
â€¢ Requiring impacted payers to report a numeric count for certain non-drug prior 
authorization metrics whose reporting was finalized through the 2024 Interoperability 
and Prior Authorization Rule; 
â€¢ Requiring impacted payers to report additional metrics for non-drug items and services 
including: 
o Percent and total count when the request was denied after timeframe for review 
was extended, and 
o Percent and total count when the request was denied after appeal; and  
â€¢ Requiring impacted payers publicly report these metrics for prior authorization requests 
and determinations for prescription drugs, as well as non-drug items and services.27 
Greater transparency by payers regarding their use of prior authorization for both prescription 
drugs and non-drug items and services will allow policymakers, in Congress and in the states, to 
better understand how their constituentsâ€™ claims are being adjudicated, as well as to identify if 
certain payers are outliers in terms of types or reasons for denials. Currently, impacted payers 
for non-drug items and services are required to report certain metrics publicly on an annual 
basis.28 However, this requirement is less informative than it could be, as there is currently no 
requirement to report this information in a standard location or to provide disaggregated 
information into which or how many services were subject to prior authorization.29 This 
undermines the impact of these reporting requirements, and the ability of policymakers, 
providers, and consumers to understand how prior authorization decisions differ based on 
service.30  
In addition to adding prescription drugs to the existing reporting requirements for impacted 
payers, CMS should require more detailed and more standardized information by payers on 
which items and services - and how many total claims - are subject to prior authorization. 
Requiring insurers to report both the numeric count and percentage of total claims that were 
subject to prior authorization will provide insight into how widespread the practice is. Similarly, 
requiring payers to disaggregate their reported information by service type will allow for better 
understanding of how consumersâ€™ health needs are being subjected to prior authorization.  
Improving the reporting of prior authorization decisions will also mean that the data can be of 
better use to those who oversee trends in prior authorization decisions as well as individuals 
relying on plans for their care, and it will enable more precise, consumer-focused policies such 
as exempting specific services with high rates of approval. Doing so will streamline and improve 
patient access to care and save providers and payers time and money currently spent on 
unnecessary prior authorization requests and appeals. Families USA supports these 
requirements for payers to publicly report more information about their use of prior 
authorization. We urge CMS to also require impacted payers to report both a numeric count 
and percentage of total claims that were subject to prior authorization and require these data 
by service type, in addition to the metrics currently required. Doing so will improve 
policymakersâ€™ and advocatesâ€™ understanding of prior authorization use. 
II. D. Requirements for Issuers That Offer Small Group Market Qualified Health Plans on the 
Federally-Facilitated Small Business Health Options Program Exchanges  
7 
 
Families USA supports expanding the requirements for QHP issuers in the individual market to 
QHP issuers in the small group market on the Federally-Facilitated Small Business Health 
Options Program (FF-SHOP). In addition to the requirements discussed earlier in this rule, CMS 
proposes to apply the non-drug item and service prior authorization and interoperability 
requirements from previous rules, including requirements to support electronic prior 
authorization, data sharing via API, and to provide a specific reason for denials within 
established timeframes.31 
An estimated 3.3 million small business owners and self-employed workers enrolled in 
marketplace coverage in 2025 through the FFE.32 Under current regulations, QHPs on the FFE 
small group market are not included in interoperability and prior authorization requirements. 
This means that the people who receive marketplace coverage through the small group market 
in the 28 states that use the FFE do not have the same protections and access to information 
about their care as other marketplace plan enrollees in their state, solely because of how they 
enrolled in that coverage.33  
Families USA supports expanding the requirements in these previous final rules and this 
proposed rule to QHP issuers on the FF-SHOP, ensuring that enrollees are protected regardless 
of how they enrolled in marketplace coverage. As CMS notes in this proposed rule, every QHP 
issuer on the individual market also participates in the small group market.34 Standardizing 
the requirements for both aspects of these issuersâ€™ FFE business will both simplify their 
operations and ensure that all marketplace enrollees who gain coverage through 
HealthCare.gov are protected by the same regulations. 
III. D. Request for Information: Step Therapy  
CMS seeks comments on whether increased interoperability of information technology (IT) 
systems across payers could be used to make utilization management policies, such as step 
therapy, more transparent.35 CMS also requests comments on how improved technology and 
data sharing may facilitate step therapy determinations and improve patient experiences with 
utilization review.36 
Step therapy is a utilization tool that plans can apply to certain medications requiring an 
individual to try and â€œfailâ€ on a lower cost medication before being approved for a more 
expensive medication to treat the same condition.37 In a 2021 article from Health Affairs, it was 
reported that 38.9 percent of commercial plans had a step therapy policy in their prescription 
drug coverage; the same report showed that when looking at ten specific diseases, almost 56 
percent of step therapy policies were more stringent that clinical guidelines.38 Some diseases, 
such as psoriasis (99.4 percent) and multiple sclerosis (88.5 percent), overwhelmingly had 
policies that were more stringent. 39  
While step therapy â€“ like prior authorization â€“ may result in lowering health care costs and 
limiting the use of low quality services or medication, it may also result in delay of the 
medications that individuals need and/or result in worse health outcomes.40 A study by the 
Alliance for Patient Access found frequent negative experiences with step therapy by patients: 
nearly 60 percent of patients who went through step therapy experienced a complication, 
8 
 
including nearly 1 in 10 who were hospitalized due to these complications. 41 Even worse, about 
half of patients only found out that they were required to try a different drug at the pharmacy 
counter.42 Transparency into how step therapy is being applied is crucial for patients and 
providers who are seeking access to needed prescription medications.  
Additionally, many patients are required to go through the step therapy process again when 
switching insurers. For example, a survey by the Arthritis Foundation found that nearly a quarter 
of patients who switched insurance providers were required to repeat step therapy.43 This 
process is frustrating and confusing for patients, in addition to the potential health impacts 
resulting from disruptions in a medication regimen that is currently working for them. 44 
Widespread adoption of electronic prior authorization, combined with the API requirements 
under this proposed rule, would enable patients and providers to better understand payersâ€™ 
utilization management policies, including changes in those policies when patients change from 
one payer to another. We urge CMS to establish transparency and communication 
requirements for payers to better understand how they are applying step therapy, including 
requirements to inform patients in a timely manner of any step therapy required by the payer. 
We also encourage CMS to require payers to incorporate and honor previous payersâ€™ step 
therapy decisions through enhanced data sharing between payers using the payer-to-payer 
API, rather than requiring providers to submit historical records or attest to prior drug 
regimens. As part of these efforts, we urge CMS to establish a uniform definition of step 
therapy, enabling state policymakers to more consistently apply consumer protections.  
Comment Solicitation of Future Rulemaking (I. C) 
CMS requests comment on whether they should pursue future rulemaking to apply the prior 
authorization transparency, interoperability, and reporting requirements proposed for QHP 
issuers on FFEs under the 2026 proposed rule, as well as similar requirements finalized under 
the 2020 CMS Interoperability and Patient Access and the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization final rules, to QHP issuers on state-based exchanges (SBEs), including state-based 
exchanges using the federal platform (SBE-FPs).45 
Families USA encourages CMS to issue future rulemaking applying the requirements of this 
proposed rule and previous final rules to QHP issuers on state-based exchanges. More than 
7.6 million consumers are enrolled in marketplace coverage in SBE states.46 Currently, federal 
regulations establishing patient safeguards and improving the efficiency of the health care 
system do not apply to these consumers, undermining the benefit of this coverage. 
Establishing uniform requirements for QHP issuers regardless of the state in which they operate, 
will improve patient experience with the health care system, improve providersâ€™ ability to 
advocate for their patients, and simplify the business operations of these issuers, similar to the 
expansion of existing and proposed requirements to QHP issuers on the FF-SHOP. Ensuring that 
a patientâ€™s health care data is accessible by every provider they see and travels with them 
seamlessly if they change insurance provider should be the ultimate goal of interoperability 
policy. This proposed rule represents a strong step toward and reaffirms CMSâ€™ commitment to 
that goal. 
9 
 
In addition to expanding these requirements to QHP issuers in the FF-SHOP, CMS should work 
with the Department of Labor (DOL) to further align interoperability and prior authorization 
requirements between the impacted payers under this rule and with the private insurance 
regulated under the Employee Retirement and Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). About half 
of all Americans receive health coverage through an employer, and these plans are not subject 
to this proposed rule or the 2020 and 2024 final rules.47 Working with DOL to ensure that the 
requirements for ERISA-regulated plans and impacted payers would ensure that all consumers 
are protected and can receive the care they need without delay or insurer red tape. 
Families USA urges CMS to issue future rulemaking to make prior authorization requirements 
across payers as uniform as possible. Future rulemaking should:  
â€¢ Extend the requirements of this proposed rule, the 2020 CMS Interoperability and 
Patient Access final rule, and the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization 
final rule to QHP issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs; 
â€¢ Be closely aligned with the Department of Labor so as to issue more detailed 
rulemaking related to prior authorization timing and transparency requirements to 
ERISA-regulated plans using DOLâ€™s ERISA statutory authority; and 
â€¢ CMS and DOL should issue joint rulemaking to align the process and timeline 
requirements across payer types. This joint rulemaking should adopt the most 
consumer-friendly timeframes and requirements from current regulations and this 
proposed rule, such as requiring all prescription drug prior authorization 
determinations to be made within 24 hours. 
Families USA applauds CMS for their continued efforts to improve provider and patient 
experience with prior authorization decisions and improve transparency. For more information 
or questions, please contact Thomas Waldrop (twaldrop@familiesusa.org), Senior Policy 
Analyst. 
Sincerely,  
 
 
Anthony Wright 
Executive Director

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Families USA; signed by Anthony Wright, Executive Director
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** National, nonpartisan health care consumer advocacy organization with 45 years of work toward affordable, high-quality coverage and care.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Families USA generally supports the proposed rule as an important step toward data-sharing standards, prior authorization transparency, and faster access for the more than 142 million people relying on Medicaid, Medicare, and marketplace coverage. It asks CMS to strengthen the rule by standardizing denial explanations, tightening drug PA timeframes toward 24 hours, improving public reporting by service type and claim volume, extending requirements to additional markets, and addressing step therapy and plan-transition harms.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; GENERAL/RFI on step therapy and future rulemaking.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 pages 19923, 19925-19927, 19933, 19936, 19938, 19940-19941, 19949, and 20013; prior 2020 and 2024 CMS interoperability rules; ERISA referenced for DOL authority.
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization APIs; national data-sharing and interoperability standards; electronic prior authorization; no detailed comments on specific FHIR IG versions or NCPDP standards.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Families USA states that electronic PA can reduce administrative cost and speed access to needed prescription and physician-administered drugs. It cites evidence that electronic PA reduced median time from request to decision from 18.7 hours to 5.7 hours.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the expansion of existing ePA requirements to prescription and physician-administered drugs for impacted payers beginning October 1, 2027.

**Topic 2: Specific Reasons for Drug PA Denials**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Denials are widespread and often overturned on appeal, suggesting inappropriate or overly aggressive prior authorization practices. Specific explanations help patients and providers pursue appeals or alternative treatments.
- **Specific request:** Provide more explicit guidance on what qualifies as a specific reason and require clinical criteria supporting denials for both drug and non-drug services.

**Topic 3: Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Current timeframes vary by payer, and delays can harm patients. Families USA supports the proposed timeframes but says CMS should adopt tighter, consumer-friendly standards where possible.
- **Specific request:** Finalize proposed timeframes and consider requiring all prescription drug PA determinations to be made within 24 hours.

**Topic 4: Public Reporting of PA Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Current PA metric reporting is not standardized enough to show which services are subject to PA or how payer decisions vary. Better data would support oversight, advocacy, and policies to exempt services with high approval rates.
- **Specific request:** Require both numeric counts and percentages of total claims subject to PA, disaggregated by service type, in addition to proposed drug and non-drug metrics.

**Topic 5: FF-SHOP Small Group QHP Requirements and Future Market Alignment**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with expansion
- **Rationale:** Consumers should receive comparable protections regardless of coverage source. The comment says SHOP and other marketplace coverage should not be left behind while employer-sponsored coverage remains outside the rule.
- **Specific request:** Extend requirements to FF-SHOP issuers, pursue future rulemaking for QHP issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs, and work with DOL to align requirements for ERISA-regulated plans.

**Topic 6: Step Therapy and Plan Transitions**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy can delay needed care, especially when patients who already completed or failed prior steps must repeat them after switching coverage.
- **Specific request:** Use future rulemaking and interoperability infrastructure to prevent unnecessary step therapy repetition, protect continuity, and apply consumer-friendly prior authorization timelines and transparency standards across payer types.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Families USA supports electronic PA for physician-administered drugs under the medical benefit, emphasizing faster decisions and reduced burden.
- **S14:** The comment supports electronic PA for pharmacy-benefit prescription drugs for impacted payers.
- **S16:** Families USA supports specific denial reasons but asks CMS to define required information more clearly and require clinical criteria supporting denials.
- **S17:** The commenter does not specifically request structured denial codes, but its request for standardized, explicit denial information aligns with structured and comparable denial communication.
- **S20:** Families USA supports proposed drug PA decision timeframes and urges CMS to consider the most consumer-friendly standard, including 24-hour prescription drug determinations.
- **S29:** The commenter supports public PA metrics for drugs and non-drug services.
- **S34:** Families USA supports improving reporting levels and deadlines, and asks for more standardized data that includes counts and percentages.
- **S35:** The comment supports public reporting that allows policymakers, providers, consumers, and advocates to identify payer outliers and denial patterns.
- **S40:** Families USA supports extending interoperability and PA requirements to small group market QHP issuers on FF-SHOPs.
- **S41:** The comment supports applying these protections in the small group market and does not seek a delay beyond the proposed framework.
- **S66-S82:** Families USA addresses step therapy and future rulemaking, urging CMS and DOL to standardize consumer protections and prevent insurer red tape from delaying medically necessary care.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize expansion of electronic prior authorization requirements to prescription and physician-administered drugs.
2. Require clear, standardized denial explanations that include clinical criteria.
3. Finalize and consider tightening decision timeframes, including 24-hour determinations for all prescription drug PA requests.
4. Require public PA metrics for drugs and non-drug services with both counts and percentages.
5. Require reporting of how many total claims and which service types are subject to PA.
6. Disaggregate PA metrics by service type.
7. Extend interoperability and PA requirements to QHP issuers in the FF-SHOP small group market.
8. Pursue future rulemaking extending similar protections to QHP issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs.
9. Work with DOL to align timing and transparency requirements for ERISA-regulated employer plans.
10. Use future policy to address step therapy repetition and continuity problems when patients change coverage.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Prior authorization misuse and overuse, unclear denial reasons, delays in care, inadequate public metrics, lack of cross-payer uniformity, and step therapy barriers.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Patients paying more than expected, declines in health, delayed care, inability to receive recommended care, abandoned care, life-threatening events, and medically necessary care denied or delayed.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Variation across payer types, insufficient specificity in denial requirements, fragmented reporting locations and metrics, lack of service-level data, and limits of CMS jurisdiction over ERISA plans without DOL coordination.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** More than 142 million people rely on Medicaid, Medicare, and marketplace coverage; about 1 in 6 insured patients report PA problems; 37% paid more than expected, 26% reported health decline, 32% reported delays, and 34% could not receive recommended care; 17% of marketplace enrollees and 22% of Medicaid beneficiaries reported PA challenges; patients taking prescription drugs were more than twice as likely to report PA problems; nearly 60% of physicians said PA always or often delays care; MA plans denied roughly 8% of PA requests in 2024 and over 80% of appealed denials were overturned; electronic PA reduced median request-to-decision time from 18.7 to 5.7 hours.
- **Studies or research referenced:** KFF coverage and PA surveys; Commonwealth Fund coverage denial survey; AMA prior authorization survey; Journal of the American Pharmacists Association evaluation of electronic PA; KFF analyses of MA and marketplace denials; Health Affairs study on step therapy protocols; legal and policy research on step therapy; Institute for Patient Access and Arthritis Foundation materials.
- **Examples provided:** Marketplace enrollees, Medicaid beneficiaries, privately insured patients, patients taking prescription drugs, small business and self-employed marketplace enrollees, patients subject to step therapy, and ERISA-covered workers.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients and families, providers, impacted payers, QHP issuers, small employers, policymakers, advocates, DOL-regulated employer plans, and CMS.
- **Economic implications:** The comment argues electronic PA and unnecessary PA exemptions can save provider and payer time and money; it also highlights consumer financial harm from delays and denials.
- **Technical feasibility:** Families USA views electronic PA and standardized reporting as feasible and beneficial, but calls for broader alignment across payers and markets.
- **Patient care impact:** Strong emphasis on faster medication access, fewer delays, clearer appeals, and reducing inappropriate denials of medically necessary care.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with recommended strengthening
- **Tone:** Professional, consumer-focused, evidence-based
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Families USA generally supports the proposed rule" - Context: Overall position on CMS-0062-P.
2. "Electronic prior authorization helps patients more quickly access the prescription drugs they need" - Context: Support for extending ePA to drugs.
3. "CMS should establish clear requirements for what information must be included when a payer denies a claim" - Context: Request for stronger denial-reason standards.
4. "requiring all prescription drug prior authorization determinations to be made within 24 hours" - Context: Future alignment and consumer-friendly timeframe recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports proposed timeframes and seeks tighter 24-hour prescription drug standards.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses administrative costs, consumer financial exposure, and potential savings from reducing unnecessary PA.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Cites physician survey data and supports ePA to reduce administrative burden.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Focuses on Medicaid, marketplace, small group, and ERISA-covered consumers needing uniform protections.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports electronic PA and better data reporting as practical tools for reducing delays.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme: timely access to medically necessary care and prescription drugs.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for CMS-DOL joint rulemaking and cross-payer alignment.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong focus on denial reasons and public PA metrics.
- [x] **FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS** - Supports extending requirements to small group market QHP issuers on FF-SHOPs.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses appeals, payer reporting, and current inconsistent PA practices.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Does not address maturity of specific standards.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - ERISA/DOL authority is discussed for future rulemaking, but not as an objection to CMS authority.
- [ ] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Supports both drug channels but does not focus on the distinction.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed.
